title: RBA believes it is done hiking interest rates, but Michele Bullock doesn't want us to think that
full_text:
Every second meeting, the Reserve Bank's boffins produce a set of economic forecasts that guides the board's thinking for the next three months.
The latest set of forecasts is good news for mortgage borrowers fearing further rate hikes.
Inflation was dramatically lower than the RBA expected just three months ago in May, even though oil prices behaved much as expected.
What's more, the bank continues to expect inflation to fall to the mid-point of its 2-3 per cent target range by the end of 2027, even though rates are tipped to be lower.
The RBA uses market pricing for future interest rates in its forecasts, so as not to given any hints about its own forward view, and traders now expect the cash rate to be about the same at the end of the forecast period in December 2028 as it is now — 4.35 per cent.
The Reserve Bank's governor Michele Bullock, learning from the mistakes of her predecessor Philip Lowe, is always reticent about giving so-called forward guidance on interest rates, that is a view on where they'll likely be at some point in the future.
At today's press conference, she came about as close to doing so as I have ever heard.
Referring to the bank's forecast that inflation would be at the mid-point of the target band by the end of 2027, she said, "This is a reasonable time to get inflation back down to target."
Reading between the lines, that tells you that if the economy continues tracking close to the RBA's current forecasts then it will see no need for further rate rises.
'May be a need for further interest rate rises'
But before borrowers break out the champagne, or trade the baked beans for Wagyu and shiraz, Ms Bullock used much of her press conference to emphasise that higher rates aren't off the table just yet.
"We'll still need to see some further progress before the board can be confident we're going to get inflation back to target with current monetary policy settings," she said.
"In waiting, the board isn't ruling out there may be a need for further interest rate rises if we look like we're off a path that takes us with inflation remaining above the target for much longer in the forecasts."
Just to make sure there was no doubt, Ms Bullock reiterated that a reduction in rates was not even discussed at the board meeting, as well as offering her personal view.
"We already raised three times, and we will go again if we need to. And I think personally that it's quite possible we may need to go, but we will wait and see what the data tells us."
For those of us attending the Statement on Monetary Policy and briefed by the RBA's chief economist Sarah Hunter, it's clear why Michele Bullock is at pains to keep a rate hike firmly on the table.
There's a litany of upside risks to the RBA's inflation forecasts, the realisation of any of which could delay the return to target beyond a "reasonable time" and see the bank hike again.
The global economy could keep growing more strongly than expected.
The Middle East oil crisis could flare up or keep dragging on, sending oil prices back over $US100 a barrel.
The energy price shock we've already had might only just be filtering through to broader price rises, especially with the fuel excise cut having temporarily mitigated some of the pain.
The capacity constraints in the economy could worsen rather than improve, with productivity again going backwards and the RBA lowering its already weak forecasts.
That weak productivity is already evident in stubborn domestic inflation, such as in the services sector, while the data centre construction boom threatens to soak up scarce tradies and push building costs to yet fresh heights.
To top it off, the looming El Niño risks slashing food production and raising prices.
Complacency the biggest inflation threat
Meanwhile, there's just one major downside risk to inflation identified by the RBA, which is a deeper-than-expected housing market downturn that dents residential building demand and sees nervy home owners close their wallets as prices keep falling.
In the presser, Bullock herself said repeatedly that housing is not the bank's focus right now.
"That isn't really the main game here for us at the moment," she told reporters.
"The main game here for us is excess capacity, tight labour market, particularly in some areas like construction, the Middle East conflict, the AI boom, these are all the things that are front of mind in terms of risks to the inflation outlook."
With most of the risks to the upside, Michele Bullock was most keen to address the greatest risk of all — complacency.
"It's important that people believe we will act if we need to," she said.
At this point, the Reserve Bank's greatest enemy is a widespread expectation that there won't be any further rate hikes.
Well-practised in jawboning, the RBA governor was today playing the role of a financial Jaws: "Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the market …", as they would say in the movie.
Bullock knows full well that further rate hikes risk pushing unemployment above 5 per cent and tipping the economy into recession.
The RBA board will take that risk if it has to, but it would rather not.
